CLASS B, REFERENCE-FREE. No product and no branding is in frame, so no reference image is sent and no product_desc is given. That is deliberate per the art-direction rule that a shot receiving no references must be asked for MATERIAL, never for identity — and it is what makes FLUX.2 safe to include here, since it has nothing to invent a brand on.

GRAPHITE MEANS A DARK REAL SCENE, NOT A STUDIO SWEEP. This is the lesson the contact and shipping banners cost: asking for 'a seamless graphite studio sweep' produced a flat colour fill, which is not a photograph. The house graphite is a real room with depth and texture — the-science is a graphite bench, copper-peptide-research a dark lab. So both slots are real interiors lit low, with the ground falling to #1A1A1A in the corners rather than being a backdrop.

3:2 LANDSCAPE, 2048x1360. Measured on the live page: multi-column renders a block image at its NATURAL aspect ratio — no wrapper ratio, no object-fit, so nothing is cropped and the master's own shape is what shows. The rendered column is 616px at 1440, so 2048 wide covers retina with room to spare. 1360 is divisible by 16 for gpt-image, which 400s on any dimension that is not.

NO LEGIBLE TEXT ANYWHERE, and this is the highest-risk part. Both scenes naturally contain documents and instruments. Any word an engine renders here would be invented regulatory text on a page about regulatory compliance, which is the worst possible place for it. So text is specified as being OUTSIDE THE DEPTH OF FIELD rather than 'too small to read' — the documented fix, since 'small' still gets drawn as letters. FLUX.2 additionally renders printed graduation digits on lab glassware on every glassware wave it has run here despite being negated, so check its candidates at full size before use.

NO FACES CARRYING THE SHOT. Slot 1 shows hands only. Slot 2's inspector is gowned and masked and turned to her work, which is both what a real cleanroom requires and a way to avoid the beauty-casting burden this project carries on face waves.

slots.title: EU Cosmetics Regulation — the safety assessment before sale
slots.prompt: Editorial photograph, landscape, of a cosmetic safety assessor's desk in a quiet laboratory office at the end of the day. On a dark graphite worktop with visible fine texture, an open ring-bound technical dossier lies square to the camera, its pages dense with body text and small data tables that fall entirely OUTSIDE the depth of field and read purely as soft grey typographic texture with no word anywhere resolvable. A pair of steel-rimmed reading glasses rests folded on the upper page. A single small clear glass sample vial with a plain unlabelled aluminium cap stands to the right, holding a colourless liquid, catching one bright specular highlight. A person's hands enter from the lower right, one resting flat on the page and the other holding a slim black pen a centimetre above the paper, poised and still, not writing; the hands are an adult's, unadorned, with short clean natural nails and real skin texture. Behind the desk the room falls away into darkness with one out-of-focus laboratory cabinet just readable as a shape. The ground is deep graphite #1A1A1A at the corners, never a flat fill: it is a real room with depth and air. One large soft key from the upper left rakes across the paper so the sheet's own surface texture and slight curl are visible, with one dim cool fill on the shadow side. 50mm at f2.8, shallow focus with the near page edge and the glasses sharp, fine film grain, restrained and expensive, no colour in the scene beyond graphite, steel and paper white.
slots.negative_extra: readable words, headings, paragraphs in focus, a signed signature, a certificate, an official stamp, coloured folders, sticky notes, a computer screen, a keyboard, a phone, coffee cup, plant, window light, daylight office

slots.title: Good Manufacturing Practice — an inspector auditing the facility
slots.prompt: Editorial photograph, landscape, inside a cosmetics manufacturing room at night, of a quality inspector auditing the plant. She stands three-quarters turned away from the camera in a clean white coverall gown with the hood up, a face mask and blue nitrile gloves, so her face is largely hidden and her attention is entirely on her work; she holds a slim clipboard low in one hand and has the other resting lightly on the rim of a large brushed stainless steel mixing vessel, checking it. The vessel dominates the left of the frame, its curved flank throwing one long soft specular highlight; behind her, out of focus, run further steel tanks, a clamped pipe manifold and a low steel gantry, receding into darkness so the room clearly continues beyond the light. The ground is deep graphite #1A1A1A, and it is a real industrial room with depth, dust in the air and reflection on a sealed dark floor, never a backdrop and never a bright white pharmaceutical cleanroom. Lighting is low and motivated: one hard cool key from a high fitting camera-left that models the steel and the shoulder of her gown, one dim cool fill from the right, and small distant practical lights falling away behind. Everything is scrupulously clean and in order. 35mm at f2.8, shallow focus with the inspector and the vessel rim sharp, fine film grain, cool neutral palette of graphite, steel and white gown, quiet and serious.
